title: Non-canonical function of transcription cofactor MLL1 in cancer
text:
Chromatin modifying enzymes are frequently mutated in cancers that lead to
dysregulation of important cellular functions. Among them, the histone methyltransferase
MLL1 has both loss of function mutations and copy number gains in cancer. Elucidating
how MLL1 contributes to tumorigenesis highlights its multifaceted roles in tumorigenesis
and facilitates development of new therapeutic strategies.

title: Personalized Vaccines Targeting Cryptic Antigens in Ovarian Cancer
text:
Even though the host anti-tumor immune response is highly active in high grade serous ovarian cancer
(HGSOC), this group of neoplasms responds poorly to current immunotherapies such as immune checkpoint
blockade. Building on our recent proteogenomic analysis showing that a group of poorly understood molecules
called “cryptic antigens” is the most abundant class of antigens recognized by the endogenous immune response
in HGSOC, we now propose to investigate whether personalized vaccines targeting cryptic antigens can
enhance anti-tumor immunity and inhibit HGSOC cancer progression.

title: Novel CART Cells for Treating AML
text:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is highly aggressive, and over 70% of patients with AML eventually become
refractory to chemotherapy and face a dire prognosis. There is a sorely unmet need to develop more effective
immunotherapy to improve AML therapy. Our proposed studies to develop the nanobody-directed, bispecific and
inducible CAR T approach aims to establish a novel and safe CART system to cure AML.

title: Defining Dysbiosis and Mechanisms of Periodontitis Progression and Stability
text:
Despite advances in our knowledge of the causes and risk factors associated with periodontitis, it remains
widely prevalent. The total expenditure on treating and preventing periodontal diseases is estimated in billions
of dollars. Determining microbial changes that lead of periodontitis progression or periodontal stability would
better inform clinicians regarding diagnosis, prevention, treatment and monitoring.

title: Assessing climate and spatial drivers of influenza dynamics across temperate and tropical settings
text:
Seasonal influenza outbreaks account for considerable morbidity and mortality each year in the US and around
the world, with disease onset timing and severity driven by factors including weather and population density.
This study will apply infectious disease modeling, machine learning methods, and statistical analysis to
investigate drivers of seasonal influenza onset and magnitude in the context of environmental and population
heterogeneity. Findings will inform outbreak preparedness efforts and advance methodological approaches to
flexibly estimate influenza transmission.

title: CAR neutrophils produced in vivo to remodel tumor microenvironment and treat glioblastoma
text:
The successful penetration of blood-brain barrier is one of the keys to successfully deliver anti-cancer
therapeutics to brain for glioblastoma treatment. This study will employ a novel strategy to precisely engineer
circulating neutrophils with chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) directly in vivo to remodel brain tumor
microenvironment and target glioblastoma, which will provide the proof-of-concept for in vivo engineered
neutrophils in targeted brain cancer therapy, having implications for other brain diseases.

title: INROADS Project 1
text: SUMMARY – Project 1: Mapping Immune Cell Responses, Outcomes, and Trajectories in a Peanut Allergy Cohort (MICRO-TRACK) Peanut allergy is a severe, persistent food allergy associated with high risk of anaphylaxis and limited treatment options. Although both peanut oral immunotherapy (OIT) and omalizumab can induce desensitization, clinical responses vary widely, and the immunologic mechanisms underlying successful treatment remain poorly defined. Moreover, the oral food challenge (OFC), the current gold standard for diagnosis and assessment of treatment efficacy, is burdensome, risky, and is impractical for routine or widespread clinical use. There is an urgent need for mechanistically informed immune biomarkers that can stratify patients, monitor therapeutic response, and serve as functional surrogates for OFC in clinical trials. Project 1, Mapping Immune Cell Responses, Outcomes and Trajectories in Peanut Allergy Cohort (MICRO- TRACK), is a multi-modal immune profiling study designed to define the systemic and allergen-specific immune trajectories associated with peanut desensitization in individuals across the full spectrum of reactivity thresholds, treated with either peanut OIT or omalizumab. Leveraging paired pre- and post-OFC blood samples collected at baseline and after one year of therapy, the study will integrate spectral flow cytometry, plasma proteomics (Olink Reveal), and allergen-specific T cell assays to uncover mechanistic and predictive signatures of therapeutic response. The central goal of MICRO-TRACK is to define cellular and proteomic immune trajectories that reflect the mechanisms of desensitization, and to identify systemic signatures predictive of clinical reactivity and therapeutic response. We hypothesize that: (i) peanut-specific T cell responses and their interaction with innate lymphoid cells are differentially modulated by therapy (Aim 1); (ii) omalizumab and peanut OIT induce distinct cellular and proteomic shifts in response to peanut challenge, shaped by their respective mechanisms of action (Aim 2); and (iii) short-term in vitro peanut stimulation of whole blood can recapitulate key features of OFC-induced immune activation and serve as a safe, scalable functional surrogate for clinical reactivity (Aim 3). The deliverables from MICRO-TRACK will include: (i) high- dimensional immune cell and protein profiles defining desensitization-specific trajectories across treatment arms; (ii) integrated allergen-specific and systemic correlates of immune modulation following OFC; and (iii) validation of an in vitro stimulation assay as a practical tool to predict OFC outcomes and therapeutic response. Together, this work will advance mechanistic insight into peanut immunotherapy and accelerate the development of biomarker-based strategies to support precision care for individuals with peanut allergy.

title: Motion-Robust Iron Quantification of Newborn Brains using Radial MRI
text:
Perinatal iron deficiency is associated with delayed nerve conduction, motor difficulties, and lower
developmental scores, with 25–85% of preterm newborns showing signs of iron deficiency during infancy.
Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) and R2* MRI offer promise for non-invasive measurement of brain
iron levels, but conventional methods are lengthy and highly motion-sensitive, limiting their use in infant
studies. We propose a novel imaging method to enable high-quality brain iron quantification in newborns,
incorporating motion-robust data acquisition, deep-learning-enhanced image reconstruction, and advanced
data analysis techniques.

title: Northwestern University Skin Disease Research Center Resource-based Center
text: The overall objective of the Administrative Core is to coordinate and oversee all activities of the SBDRC. The Administrative Core organizes opportunities for learning, networking, and communication, provides pilot grants, and schedules meetings of Center leaders, Boards and scientists at Northwestern and nationally.

title: The Carolina Endometrial Cancer Study: A population-based survivor cohort
text: More than 891,000 U.S. women have an endometrial cancer history, making it the second largest cancer survivor group among women. Disparities by race have been reported across the endometrial cancer continuum—from recognition of symptoms leading to diagnosis through receipt of guideline recommended cancer therapy and survivorship care. The Carolina Endometrial Cancer Study is a population-based cancer epidemiology survivor cohort that collects detailed information on novel molecular characteristics; medical history; cancer treatment and follow-up care; individual- and contextual-level social determinants of health; and behavioral and lifestyle factors to advance our understanding of endometrial cancer survivorship.

title: 2/3 Understanding PTSD through Postmortem Targeted Brain Multi-omics
text:
The prevalence of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression are among the most common of the
severe major psychiatric disorders. There have yet to be postmortem studies of well-matched cases and controls
to leverage the fact that these are arguably among the best understood psychiatric disorders in terms of neural
circuit regulation. Building on impactful linked R01 project, in our renewal proposal we will expand the sample
size and dive deeper with more detailed analyses of the postmortem phenotypes and more comprehensive mo-
lecular studies to identify pathways harboring potential diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

title: Modeling Minimal Residual Disease in Colorectal Cancer
text:
Relevance
Adjuvant therapy for colorectal cancer after curative surgical resection has not changed in over two decades
and to date, there have been limited studies to study the minimal residual disease that leads to recurrence and
metastasis. In our current proposal, we have used a new and novel patient derived models of colorectal
cancer termed MicroOrganoSpheres (MOS) to identity and characterize minimal residual disease. The
completion of this proposal will result in the understanding of the biology of the minimal residual disease of
resected colorectal cancer that determines recurrence and metastasis resulting in improved outcomes for
these patients.

title: Development of Quinoxaline Based IKKbeta Inhibitors for Kras Driven Cancers
text:
MAP3K1 is an emerging therapeutic target. Through an iterative synthesis and screening we identified
50-008 that targets MAP3K1 and exhibits broad anticancer activities. We expect to define the mechanism of
action and optimize 50-008 to identify a lead compound suitable for IND-enabling toxicity studies.

title: Human Imaging and Biorepository Core
text: CORE D: PROJECT SUMMARY The overall goal for the Human Resources and Biomedical Imaging Core (Core D) is to facilitate human-based studies addressing the Cedars-Sinai Digestive Diseases Research Center (CSDDRC) theme of mechanisms and measurements of the fibroinflammatory response in gastrointestinal (GI) tissues. Core D will provide new services and resources that are not currently available to members of the CSDDRC. The services and resources will support new and existing federally funded projects to accelerate key achievements toward understanding how fibro-inflammatory biology contributes to the initiation and progression of these diseases. Core D will create unique resources to assist CSDDRC member investigations and collaborations including prospective collections and associated metadata as well as improving access to already available resources in biospecimens and human imaging databases. In Aim 1, Core D will support human biospecimen research by establishing a Core D/(Biobank and Research Pathology) BRP partnership. By allocating Core D staff resources into an integrated intestine/liver/pancreas biobanking service, center members will have access to collection services distinguished by comprehensiveness (recruitment and consent under the master BRP IRB, collection and processing of specimens and associated data, and specimen/data distribution in a research-ready de-identified format) at a subsidized 25% discount and staffing at relevant clinics and procedure suites. In addition, Core D will establish a Biorepositories Searchable Databases Resource, permitting summary, deidentified inspection of biorepository content for biospecimens, clinical- and meta-data. In Aim 2, Core D will support human imaging research by establishing a Core D/Biomedical Imaging Research Institute BIRI partnership to provide services for imaging collection, data management of clinical images, and affiliated clinical data. It will also provide complementary pilot radiomic analysis services, and prospective research image acquisition at a subsidized 25% discount. Akin to Aim 1, where archival image repositories may be suitable, it will establish an Imaging Searchable Database Resource for existing imaging repositories, hosted on the CSDDRC website. Effective use of these services and resources requires careful pre-study planning to optimize feasibility of the study plan and coordinate operations between the investigator team and the Core D services and resource teams. A Pre-Study Consultation Team will provide expert input on project planning and study operational design to guide investigators regarding the optimal choice of resources, services, and analytic plans that will lead to future NIDDK grant applications and funding at no cost.

title: Immunologic strategies to prevent congenital cytomegalovirus transmission and disease in rhesus monkeys
text:
Congenital cytomegalovirus (cCMV) is the leading global infectious cause of birth defects, hearing loss, and
long-term neurologic deficits in infants exposed during gestation. Despite being considered a top priority for
several decades, development of an effective CMV vaccine has been limited due to a gap in understanding of
protective immune responses and virologic determinants of congenital CMV transmission. This Program will
identify new antigen targets and immunization strategies for CMV vaccines to prevent and reduce cCMV
infection, guiding design and clinical trial testing of next generation HCMV vaccines to prevent congenital CMV
transmission.

title: End-to-End X-ray-based Cancer Imaging Simulation Toolkit for Technology Evaluation, AI Training, and Virtual Imaging Clinical Trials
text:
We will develop the next-generation X-ray-based Cancer Imaging Simulation Toolkit (XCIST 2.0), which is the only
comprehensive x-ray and computed tomography (CT) imaging system simulation toolkit that is publicly available. We will
address critical gaps in XCIST 1.0 by including 1) physics models for photon-counting CT, phase-contrast imaging, dose
estimation, and deep learning reconstruction; 2) end-to-end capability for performing virtual cancer imaging trials and
deep learning training, including image quality phantoms, virtual lesions, and model observers; and 3) major
enhancements for improved usability, including a graphical user interface, GPU acceleration, cloud deployment,
documentation, and video tutorials. This integrated toolkit will enable and accelerate development and evaluation of
new imaging technologies for cancer imaging as well as other clinical applications.

title: Spatiotemporal Mapping of Huntington's Disease Progression through Multimodal MRI-based Circuit Analysis
text:
This proposal aims to develop a circuit-based framework to characterize spatial and temporal alterations in
Huntington’s Disease (HD) pathogenesis using advanced multimodal MRI. Focusing on two key brain networks
affected in HD, the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) and cerebello-thalamo-cortical (CTC) circuits, we will
identify domain-specific changes in brain atrophy, structural and functional connectivity, iron and myelin content,
and striatal metabolism in premanifest and early manifest HD compared to age-matched controls. By integrating
these measures, we will establish a spatial-temporal model of disease progression and symptom evolution. The
resulting insights and biomarkers will enhance individualized prediction of clinical decline and inform the design
of future disease-modifying trials.

title: A systematic study of the environmental etiology of autism spectrum disorder using high-throughput behavioral screening
text:
Both genetic and environmental risk factors play a part in the development of autism, yet despite being
estimated to account for 41% of autism risk, we know very little about what environmental factors contribute to
autism risk. Because social deficit is one of the 3 core symptoms of autism, I developed a high-throughput
screening approach to systematically search for chemicals that inhibit the development of social behavior. This
screen revealed topoisomerase II as a key regulator of the development of social behavior in zebrafish and
mouse, which is investigated in further detail in this proposal.

title: Mass Spectrometry and Proteomics
text: MASS SPECTROMETRY & PROTEOMICS MODULE The Vanderbilt Vision Research Center (VVRC) includes investigators with a strong interest in discerning how protein signatures govern functional circuits in the visual pathways and predispose patients towards disease and response to treatment. These relationships require the ability to measure protein content and patterns in large numbers of samples, transgenic animals, and even within highly localized intact tissues. The purpose of the VVRC Mass Spectrometry & Proteomics Module is to provide a comprehensive resource for all mass spectrometry needs for investigators needing proteomics, metabolomics, or tissue imaging via mass spectrometry. This module provides access to state-of-the-art mass spectrometry, proteomics, and mass spectrometry tissue imaging facilities via subsidized scholarship use of the Vanderbilt Mass Spectrometry Research Center (MSRC). The MSRC comprises the Mass Spectrometry Core Laboratory, the Proteomics Laboratory, and the Tissue Imaging Core, all with bioinformatic support through the MSRC Bioinformatics Group. VVRC support translates on a dollar-for-dollar basis to scholarships issued to VVRC investigators applicable for all MSRC services. This scholarship system is implemented by the VUMC Office of Research and is utilized instead of a discount or co-pay via the VUMC ILab accounting system. In the current funding cycle, the Proteomics Service Module was used by 12 investigators who authored 142 publications using the service, including 6 current NEI R01 holders. In the next cycle, we expect moderate to extensive use by 22 of 52 VVRC faculty members, including 9 of 16 current NEI R01 grant holders. The Mass Spectrometry & Proteomics Module, housed in a centralized location conveniently accessed from all parts of campus, is directed by Professor Kevin Schey, PhD, who also directs a subset of the MSRC housed cores. Using resources and personnel supported in part by this core grant, the VVRC Mass Spectrometry & Proteomics Module will assist in (1) experimental design for proteomics, metabolomics, or imaging mass spectrometry projects and (2) preparation of visual system tissues for mass spectrometry analysis and provide (3) comprehensive proteomics service, (4) a range of small molecule and metabolomics services, (5) access to imaging mass spectrometry (IMS) services, and (6) training to members of the vision research community in LC-MS or IMS techniques. These services and resources will enhance the scope of experimentation NEI- funded VVRC investigators conduct, expand the training of students and fellows involved in vision science, and promote collaboration by providing sophisticated, high-resolution and high-throughput proteomics and bioinformatic services to those who otherwise would not have such capabilities, including early-career vision scientists and clinician-scientists competing for extramural funding for their laboratories.

title: CRCNS: Discovering Computational Principles of Language Processing in the Brain
text: A critical characteristic of human language is our ability to understand multi-word sequences whose meaning is greater than the sum of their parts. Recent work from the PIs of this proposal (Toneva and Wehbe, 2019; Jain and Huth, 2018) and others (Schrimpf et al., 2020a; Caucheteux & King, 2020) has shown that cortical representations of multi-word sequences can be modeled much more accurately than before by using neural network language models, a machine learning technique that has revolutionized the natural language processing (NLP) field (Devlin et al., 2019; Radford et al., 2019). However, under the current paradigm these models must first be trained on separate NLP tasks and only then used to model the brain, creating a guess-and-check cycle that is not guaranteed to converge on the actual computations that humans perform. Here we propose to break this cycle by directly training neural network models to estimate the functions that the brain uses to combine words. To be able to optimally predict fMRI and MEG responses, these models will need to capture the composition principles governing which words the brain attends to, and how information is combined across words. These models will help uncover specific computations underlying language processing in the brain, enable computational testing of neurolinguistic theories, and inspire or directly improve models used in NLP. Accomplishing these goals, however, will require overcoming one major obstacle. Training neural net- work language models typically requires orders of magnitude more data than existing neuroimaging datasets. To address this issue, one central goal of this proposed project is to collect a very large fMRI and MEG dataset comprising roughly one million words of natural language stimuli. We plan to use the unique dataset and computational modeling framework to address three scientific aims. Aim 1: Create brain activity prediction benchmarks to foster interaction between neuroscience and NLP. Aim 2: Use data-driven models to test existing neurolinguistic theories & develop new accounts of the computations underlying word composition in the brain. Aim 3: Leverage information in different brain areas to help solve computationally defined language tasks. Successful completion of the proposed work will provide mechanistic insight into language processing, with a computational architecture tracing information flow among brain areas and describing the tasks they perform. Beyond its basic cognitive neuroscience implications, we expect this work will enable better understanding of language impairments and help identify targeted therapies. RELEVANCE (See instructions): Through collecting, analyzing, and disseminating large-scale neuroimaging datasets collected while participants listen to natural, narrative speech, this proposal aims to improve our understanding of the normal function of the language system. Specifically, this work seeks to improve and validate computational models of speech language processing in the human brain.
